name: Neutron
info: An atomic nucleus, or a [em1]nuclide[em1], is made of [em2]protons[em2] and [em3]neutrons[em3]. Protons have a positive charge to counteract the negative charge of [em2]electrons[em2] that orbit in shells around the nucleus. Neutrons have [em3]zero[em3] [em3]charge[em3]; that is to say they are neutral.[br] [br]More neutrons in a nucleus do not change an element's chemical properties but they do make it [em1]heavier[em1] and they can affect how [em2]stable[em2] the nuclide is. Nuclides that are not stable [em2]decay[em2] into other nuclides. The measure for how long a given nuclide will last is called its [em3]half-life[em3]. Nuclides decay [em1]at random[em1] so it's impossible to know exactly when a particular nuclide will decay. Instead, how long it takes about half of a bunch of the same nuclide to decay is measurable, and that's what half-life means.[br] [br]The nuclide that is a lone free neutron, [link]Neutron-1[link], has a half-life of about 10 minutes. This means if you had 1000 free neutrons then after ten minutes you could expect to have only 500, and only 250 left after 20 minutes. Neutrons can be stable when combined with protons inside an [em1]atomic nucleus[em1].

name: Hydrogen
info: As the very first element [em3]Hydrogen[em3] has only one proton. It's not just first on the Periodic Table, though, it's literally [em1]the first element to exist[em1]. To this day [em2]75% of all the matter in the universe is Hydrogen[em2].[br] [br]Hydrogen on its own is usually a [em1]gas[em1]. The two H's in [em3]H[sub]2[sub]O[em3] are the two Hydrogen atoms, combined with one Oxygen atom, to make [em2]water[em2]. In many common reactions between [em1]acids (like vinegar - C[sub]2[sub]H[sub]4[sub]O[sub]2[sub])[em1] and [em2]bases[em2] [em2](like baking soda - NaHCO[sub]3[sub])[em2], the acid gives a Hydrogen to the base.[br] [br]Hydrogen has two stable isotopes: [link]Hydrogen-1[link] with zero neutrons, also called [em3]Protium[em3], and [link]Hydrogen-2[link] with one neutron, also called [em3]Deuterium[em3] (remember: the number comes from the sum of neutrons and protons). With two neutrons, [link]Hydrogen-3[link] also has a special name: [em3]Tritium[em3]. Tritium has a [em1]half-life[em1] of 12.32 years, making it the most stable [em1]radioisotope[em1] of Hydrogen (isotopes that are [em2]radioactive[em2] and decay). All the other isotopes of Hydrogen are very unstable and have half-lives that are only fractions of a second.

name: Helium
info: [em3]Helium[em3] is the lightest [em2]noble gas[em2], meaning it is both incredibly light and very non-reactive. In fact, to make [em1]compounds[em1] with Helium and other elements, it usually requires extreme temperatures or pressures.[br] [br]While Helium is the [em2]second most abundant[em2] element in the universe after [link]Hydrogen[link] it is somewhat rare on Earth because it is so light and non-reactive that it tends to float up to the top of the atmosphere and [em2]escape to space[em2]. Helium also has the lowest [em1]boiling point[em1] of any element, meaning its liquid state is incredibly cold [em2](around 4.2 K, or ​−452° F / −269° C)[em2]. This makes liquid Helium ideal for applications that require extremely low temperatures, such as the [em3]superconducting magnets[em3] used in MRI machines, particle accelerators, and quantum computers.[br] [br]When an atomic nucleus decays by [em3]Alpha (α) decay[em3] it emits an Alpha particle, composed of two [em1]neutrons and two protons[em1]... the same thing as a [link]Helium-4[link] nucleus. This reduces the parent nucleus's atomic number by two, for example turning [link]Uranium-238[link] into [link]Thorium-234[link] + [link]Helium-4[link].

name: Lithium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Lithium[em3] is the lightest metal, [em2]light enough to float on water[em2] and soft enough to cut with a knife. Most of it was [em1]made in the Big Bang itself[em1], along with [link]Hydrogen[link] and [link]Helium[link], though old stars hold less of it than theory predicts, a puzzle called the 'cosmological lithium problem'.[br] [br]Lithium is the [em3]heart of the rechargeable battery[em3]. About 88% of it goes into batteries for phones, laptops, electric vehicles, and grid storage, and world production has passed 200,000 metric tons a year, led by Australia, China, and Chile. Much of it comes from brine pumped into [em2]evaporation ponds on salt flats[em2] in South America.[br] [br]Since 1949 Lithium salts have been used as a mood stabilizer, and they remain [em1]a leading treatment for bipolar disorder[em1]. Lithium hydroxide scrubs carbon dioxide from the air in spacecraft and submarines.[br] [br][link]Lithium-6[link] is used to breed [link]Hydrogen-3[link] (tritium) for nuclear weapons and [em3]future fusion reactors[em3]. In 1932 Lithium became the first element split by a [em2]fully human-made nuclear reaction[em2], when protons fired at [link]Lithium-7[link] produced two [link]Helium-4[link] nuclei.

name: Beryllium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Beryllium[em3] is light but [em2]about 35% stiffer than steel[em2], and it's [em1]nearly transparent to X-rays[em1], so it's the most common window material in X-ray equipment. Like [link]Boron[link], it isn't made by fusion inside stars but mostly by [em2]cosmic rays breaking apart heavier atoms[em2] in interstellar space.[br] [br]Only about 220 metric tons are produced each year, nearly all in the US, China, and Kazakhstan, mostly from the mineral beryl, whose gem forms are [em3]emerald and aquamarine[em3]. Beryllium [link]Copper[link], about 2% Beryllium, is six times stronger than Copper alone. The [em1]James Webb Space Telescope[em1] has 18 gold-plated Beryllium mirror segments that hold their shape at -240°C.[br] [br][em2]Inhaled Beryllium dust is dangerous.[em2] It can cause berylliosis, a chronic and sometimes fatal lung disease whose symptoms can take years to appear, and fluorescent lamps stopped using Beryllium compounds after workers fell ill.[br] [br]Short-lived [link]Beryllium-8[link] is a stepping stone inside stars: through it, three [link]Helium-4[link] nuclei fuse to form [link]Carbon-12[link], the [em3]carbon that life is built on[em3].

name: Boron
info: [em3]Boron[em3] has five protons and isn't made by [em1]fusion inside stars[em1]. Instead it comes from [em1]cosmic ray spallation[em1], where high-energy cosmic rays break apart heavier nuclei, and from supernovas. It's rare in the solar system and makes up only about [em2]0.001% of Earth's crust by weight[em2].[br] [br]Boron has two stable isotopes: [link]Boron-11[link] (about 80% of natural boron) and [link]Boron-10[link] (about 20%). Boron-10 has a high [em2]cross-section for neutron capture[em2], meaning it's very good at [em3]absorbing neutrons[em3]. That makes boron useful in nuclear reactors, in control rods and boric acid, for fission control and emergency shutdown.[br] [br]The same property is used in medicine. In [em1]boron neutron capture therapy[em1], a Boron-10 compound is taken up by a tumor and hit with low-energy neutrons. Each capture releases an alpha particle (a [link]Helium-4[link] nucleus) and a [link]Lithium-7[link] ion, which travel only a short distance, so the damage stays close to the tumor cells.[br] [br]Boron-11 is also a candidate fuel for [em1]aneutronic fusion[em1], a kind of fusion that produces few neutrons. Hit by a proton of about 500 keV, it produces [em3]three alpha particles[em3] and [em3]8.7 MeV of energy[em3].

name: Carbon
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Carbon[em3] is the [em2]basis of all known life[em2]. Its atoms can bond with up to four others at once, forming the chains and rings of proteins, sugars, fats, and DNA. About 18.5% of your body's mass is Carbon, second only to [link]Oxygen[link]. Inside stars, three [link]Helium-4[link] nuclei fuse to make [link]Carbon-12[link].[br] [br]Pure Carbon takes very different forms. [em1]Diamond is the hardest natural substance[em1] and conducts heat better than any other, while graphite is [em3]soft enough to leave marks on paper[em3] as pencil 'lead'. Graphene, a sheet of graphite one atom thick, has been called [em2]the strongest material ever tested[em2].[br] [br]Coal, oil, and natural gas are Carbon-rich remains of ancient life. Burning them to power civilization releases [em1]carbon dioxide (CO[sub]2[sub])[em1], a greenhouse gas that traps heat, and rising CO[sub]2[sub] is [em3]the main driver of climate change[em3]. Carbon is also what turns [link]Iron[link] into steel, and carbon black colors tires and printer toner.[br] [br]Living things take in radioactive [link]Carbon-14[link] from the air until they die, so measuring what's left, called radiocarbon dating, can [em2]reveal the age of remains[em2] up to about 50,000 years old.

name: Nitrogen
info: [em3]Nitrogen[em3] is one of the most common elements in the universe. Two atoms of it bond to form diatomic Nitrogen gas (N[sub]2[sub]), which makes up [em2]78% of Earth's atmosphere[em2].[br] [br]Nitrogen occurs in all organisms, primarily in [em1]amino acids[em1] (and thus proteins), in the [em1]nucleic acids (DNA and RNA)[em1] and in the energy transfer molecule [em1]adenosine triphosphate (ATP)[em1] that powers all cells. The human body contains about 3% nitrogen by mass. Because of its importance for life Nitrogen is a key component of [em2]fertilizers[em2], usually in the form of [em2]Ammonia (NH[sub]3[sub])[em2].[br] [br]Nitrogen has many industrial applications. Due to its abundance, [em3]low boiling point (−195°C / −320°F)[em3], and low rate of evaporative loss [em3]liquid nitrogen[em3] is commonly used for cooling things to very low temperatures. This can include [em2]cryotherapies[em2] such as removing skin cysts and warts, [em2]cryopreservation[em2] of biological materials, and cooling sensitive electronics such as [em2]infrared and x-ray detectors[em2].

name: Oxygen
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Oxygen[em3] is the [em2]third most abundant element in the universe[em2], after [link]Hydrogen[link] and [link]Helium[link], forged in stars by fusing [link]Carbon[link] with Helium. On Earth it's nearly half the mass of the crust, bound up in rocks, and [em1]89% of the mass of the oceans[em1] as water (H[sub]2[sub]O).[br] [br]About [em3]21% of the air[em3] we breathe is Oxygen gas (O[sub]2[sub]), and an adult at rest inhales about 2 grams of it every minute. Every cell uses it to release energy from food. Nearly all of it was made by photosynthesis, and when it first filled the air some 2.4 billion years ago, in the [em2]Great Oxidation Event[em2], it was poisonous to much of the life that existed then.[br] [br]Around 100 million metric tons of Oxygen are separated from air each year, [em1]more than half for steelmaking[em1]. The rest goes to chemicals, welding torches, hospital oxygen therapy, and, as [em3]pale blue liquid oxygen[em3], rocket fuel.[br] [br]High in the atmosphere, three-atom ozone (O[sub]3[sub]) [em2]shields life from ultraviolet light[em2]. Liquid oxygen is [em1]magnetic enough to cling[em1] between the poles of a strong magnet.

name: Fluorine
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Fluorine[em3] is the [em1]most electronegative element[em1], meaning it pulls on electrons harder than any other atom. It reacts with nearly every element, and in a jet of Fluorine gas [em2]even wood and water burst into flame[em2]. The bond it makes with [link]Carbon[link] is the [em3]strongest in organic chemistry[em3].[br] [br]That strength is behind [em1]nonstick pans and waterproof fabrics[em1] like PTFE (Teflon), but it also makes some fluorinated chemicals, the [em2]PFAS or 'forever chemicals'[em2], extremely slow to break down in the environment. Sulfur hexafluoride, used in high-voltage electrical equipment, has the highest global warming potential of any known substance.[br] [br]Small amounts of fluoride in [em3]toothpaste and drinking water[em3] strengthen tooth enamel against decay. Roughly 20% of modern medicines contain Fluorine, including the antidepressant fluoxetine (Prozac), and radioactive [link]Fluorine-18[link] is the tracer in [em1]most PET scans[em1].[br] [br]The largest use of Fluorine gas is turning [link]Uranium[link] into uranium hexafluoride, a gas that can be [em2]enriched for nuclear fuel[em2]. Fluorine is the 13th most common element in Earth's crust, mostly in the mineral fluorite.

name: Neon
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Neon[em3] is the [em2]fifth most abundant element in the universe[em2], made inside massive stars, but it's rare on Earth at only about 18 parts per million of the air. It's one of the [em1]least reactive elements known[em1].[br] [br]In an electric field Neon [em3]glows a brilliant reddish-orange[em3], which made it famous in neon signs. Signs of other colors use other gases, like [link]Argon[link] and [link]Mercury[link] vapor, but [em2]are still called 'neon'[em2].[br] [br]Neon can only be extracted by distilling liquid air, and it's surprisingly important to modern electronics. It's the main gas in the [em1]lasers that etch computer chips[em1], and when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, cutting off a large share of the world's supply, [em3]Neon prices soared[em3]. Liquid Neon also has more than 40 times the cooling capacity of the same volume of liquid [link]Helium[link], and it's cheaper for most cooling uses.[br] [br]Neon was discovered in 1898 along with [link]Krypton[link] and [link]Xenon[link], as one of the rare gases left over in dry air. Its name is [em2]Greek for 'new'[em2].

name: Sodium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Sodium[em3] is a soft, silvery metal that [em1]explodes in contact with water[em1], so pure Sodium is stored under oil. Combined with [link]Chlorine[link], a poisonous gas, it makes something we eat every day: [em2]table salt (NaCl)[em2]. Seawater holds about 11 grams of Sodium per liter, the source of the ocean's saltiness.[br] [br]Your nerves run on Sodium. Pumps in every cell push Sodium ions out and pull [link]Potassium[link] in, and the rush back across the membrane is what [em3]fires a nerve impulse[em3]. Adults need only about 500 mg a day, but the average American eats about 3.4 grams, and [em1]too much salt raises blood pressure[em1] and the risk of heart disease and stroke.[br] [br]Heated Sodium glows bright yellow, [em2]the color of sodium-vapor street lights[em2] in cities around the world. Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) raises bread, lye (sodium hydroxide) makes soap, and salt de-ices roads.[br] [br]Liquid Sodium carries heat well and absorbs few neutrons, so it [em3]cools fast nuclear reactors[em3], and a Sodium-Potassium alloy is liquid at room temperature. Sodium's symbol Na comes from [em1]its Latin name, natrium[em1].

name: Magnesium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Magnesium[em3] sits [em2]at the center of every chlorophyll molecule[em2], so it's essential to the photosynthesis that feeds nearly all life on Earth. Your body holds about 25 grams, mostly in the skeleton, and [em1]more than 300 enzymes depend on it[em1], including those that use ATP for energy. Leafy greens, nuts, and whole grains are good sources.[br] [br]Inside aging massive stars, [em3][link]Carbon[link] and [link]Helium[link] nuclei fuse[em3] into Magnesium. It's the eighth most abundant element in Earth's crust and the [em2]third most common dissolved in seawater[em2].[br] [br]Magnesium is about [em1]two-thirds as dense as[em1] [link]Aluminium[link], and it's the third most used structural metal after [link]Iron[link] and Aluminium. It's alloyed into Aluminium for drink cans and cast into [em3]car parts, laptop cases, and aircraft components[em3]. China produces about 85% of the world's supply. Magnesium also strips [link]Sulfur[link] from steel and is used to refine [link]Titanium[link].[br] [br]Once lit, Magnesium [em2]burns with a blinding white light[em2] at about 3,100°C, which made it the flash of early photography and still lights flares and fireworks. Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate, and milk of magnesia is an antacid.

name: Aluminium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Aluminium[em3] is the [em2]most abundant metal in Earth's crust[em2], about 8% by mass, yet it was [em1]once more expensive than[em1] [link]Gold[link]. It clings so tightly to [link]Oxygen[link] that pure Aluminium was very hard to make until 1886, when an [em3]electrical smelting process[em3] was invented. French emperor Napoleon III reportedly served his most honored guests on Aluminium plates.[br] [br]Today the world makes about 72 million metric tons a year, more than half of it in China, more than any metal except [link]Iron[link]. It's [em2]about a third as dense as steel[em2], conducts electricity well, and a thin oxide layer protects it from corrosion, so it's in [em1]airplanes, cars, power lines, cans, and foil[em1].[br] [br]Smelting Aluminium takes so much electricity that smelters are often built [em3]near cheap hydroelectric power[em3]. Recycling it takes [em2]only about 5% of that energy[em2], which is why Aluminium cans are so widely recycled.[br] [br]Rubies and sapphires are [em1]crystals of aluminium oxide[em1] tinted by traces of other elements. Radioactive [link]Aluminium-26[link] in the early solar system decayed into [link]Magnesium-26[link], [em3]helping date the oldest meteorites[em3]. In the US and Canada it's spelled 'aluminum'.

name: Silicon
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Silicon[em3] is the [em2]second most abundant element in Earth's crust[em2], about 28% by mass, after [link]Oxygen[link]. The two together form silica (SiO[sub]2[sub]) and the silicate minerals that make up most rocks, along with [em1]sand and quartz[em1].[br] [br]Purified to 99.9999999%, Silicon is the [em3]foundation of the information age[em3]. It's a semiconductor, and since it replaced [link]Germanium[link] in the early 1970s nearly [em2]every computer chip, phone, and solar panel[em2] has been built on Silicon wafers, giving Silicon Valley its name. Tiny amounts of [link]Phosphorus[link] or [link]Boron[link] added to it control how it conducts.[br] [br]Most Silicon, though, goes into steel and [link]Aluminium[link] alloys. Silica sand is [em1]melted into glass[em1] and is a key ingredient of concrete and cement. Silicones, built from chains of Silicon and Oxygen, show up in sealants, cookware, and medical implants.[br] [br]Diatoms, tiny algae, [em3]build glassy shells of silica[em3], and rice uses it to strengthen its cells. Breathing in fine crystalline silica dust, though, causes [em2]silicosis, a scarring lung disease[em2] that affects miners and stone cutters.

name: Phosphorus
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Phosphorus[em3] is part of the [em2]backbone of every DNA and RNA molecule[em2], and of ATP, the molecule that carries energy in every cell. An adult body holds about 0.7 kg of it, 85 to 90% in [em1]bones and teeth[em1] as [link]Calcium[link] phosphate.[br] [br]Because all life needs it, Phosphorus is often [em3]the nutrient that limits how much crops can grow[em3], and most mined phosphate rock goes into fertilizer. Morocco holds about two-thirds of the world's exploitable reserves. Fertilizer that washes off fields can [em2]feed algae blooms[em2] that choke lakes and coastal waters.[br] [br]Pure Phosphorus comes in several forms. [em1]White Phosphorus glows faintly[em1] in the dark and bursts into flame in air at about 30°C. It's highly toxic, and 19th-century match workers developed 'phossy jaw', a rotting of the jawbone. Today's safety matches use [em3]much safer red Phosphorus[em3] on the striking strip of the box.[br] [br]Phosphorus was first isolated in 1669 by [em2]boiling down large amounts of urine[em2], and its name is Greek for 'light-bearer'. Small amounts of Phosphorus added to [link]Silicon[link] help make computer chips.

name: Sulfur
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Sulfur[em3] has been known since ancient times as [em1]brimstone, the 'burning stone'[em1] found around volcanoes. It's a bright yellow solid that [em2]melts into a blood-red liquid[em2] when burned and gives off a blue flame. It has more solid forms than any other element, the most common being a ring of eight atoms.[br] [br]Sulfur is essential to life. The amino acids cysteine and methionine contain it, and bonds between Sulfur atoms give [em3]hair and fingernails their strength[em3]. Many of the [em1]strongest smells in nature[em1] come from Sulfur compounds, including rotten eggs (hydrogen sulfide), skunk spray, garlic, and onions.[br] [br]Around 70 million metric tons are produced each year, nearly all removed from oil and natural gas, and most of it becomes sulfuric acid, [em2]one of the most produced industrial chemicals[em2] and essential for making [link]Phosphorus[link] fertilizers. Sulfur also [em3]vulcanizes rubber for tires[em3] and goes into gunpowder and matches.[br] [br]Burning fossil fuels releases sulfur dioxide, which [em1]forms acid rain[em1]. Sulfur gives Jupiter's moon Io its yellow color, and the [em2]deep blue of lapis lazuli[em2] comes from three-atom Sulfur ions.

name: Chlorine
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Chlorine[em3] is a [em2]pale yellow-green gas[em2], its name from the Greek for 'pale green'. It's a powerful oxidizer and so poisonous that it was [em1]used as a chemical weapon[em1] in World War I, starting in 1915.[br] [br]Yet bound to [link]Sodium[link] it's [em3]the table salt we eat[em3], and chloride ions are essential to all life. They help balance the body's fluids, and the hydrochloric acid in your stomach digests food. Your own immune cells even [em2]make Chlorine compounds to kill bacteria[em2].[br] [br]About 97 million metric tons of Chlorine are made each year by running electricity through salt water. [em1]Chlorinated drinking water[em1] dramatically reduced diseases like cholera and typhoid, and Chlorine bleach and pool disinfectants carry on that role. More than a third of all Chlorine goes into [em3]PVC plastic for pipes[em3], flooring, and cables, and some 15,000 Chlorine compounds are used commercially, including many medicines.[br] [br]Chlorine has a darker side in the environment. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) carried Chlorine high into the atmosphere where it [em2]destroyed the ozone layer[em2], and the pesticide DDT, another Chlorine compound, harmed bird populations.

name: Argon
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Argon[em3] makes up [em2]almost 1% of the air[em2] (0.934%), the third most abundant gas in the atmosphere and more than 20 times as common as carbon dioxide. Its name is [em1]Greek for 'lazy'[em1], because it's so unreactive that no stable compound of it is known at room temperature.[br] [br]Nearly all of Earth's Argon is [link]Argon-40[link], made over billions of years by the decay of radioactive [link]Potassium-40[link] in rocks. Geologists measure how much has built up to [em3]find the age of rocks[em3], a method called potassium-argon dating.[br] [br]About 700,000 metric tons are distilled from liquid air each year. Argon is cheap, heavy, and inert, so it's the [em1]shielding gas for welding[em1], fills light bulbs, and insulates double-pane windows. Since 2002 the US Declaration of Independence and Constitution have been kept in [em2]sealed cases filled with Argon[em2]. Because it's denser than air, though, Argon can [em1]pool in closed spaces and suffocate people[em1].[br] [br][em3]Huge tanks of liquid Argon[em3] are used in searches for dark matter and in neutrino detectors, which watch for faint flashes of light when particles strike Argon nuclei.

name: Potassium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Potassium[em3] is a soft metal [em2]light enough to float on water[em2], and it reacts with water so violently that the [link]Hydrogen[link] it releases [em1]bursts into a lilac flame[em1]. It makes up about 2.6% of Earth's crust.[br] [br]Every cell in your body depends on it. Pumps in cell membranes pull Potassium in and push [link]Sodium[link] out, and the balance between them [em3]fires nerves and keeps the heart beating[em3]. An adult holds about 120 grams, 98% of it inside cells. Potatoes, beans, and bananas are rich in it, though [em2]it would take about 11 bananas[em2] to get a full day's worth. Too much or too little Potassium in the blood can disrupt the heart's rhythm.[br] [br]About 95% of all Potassium chemicals [em1]become fertilizer, called potash[em1], mined mainly in Canada, Russia, and Belarus. Potassium nitrate (saltpeter) is [em3]the oxidizer in gunpowder[em3].[br] [br]A tiny fraction of natural Potassium is radioactive [link]Potassium-40[link], the most common radioactive nuclide in the human body and [em2]the reason bananas are slightly radioactive[em2]. Its slow decay into [link]Argon-40[link] is used to date rocks.

name: Calcium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Calcium[em3] is the [em2]most abundant metal in the human body[em2]. An adult holds about a kilogram, nearly all of it in bones and teeth as a hard mineral called hydroxyapatite. Calcium ions also act as messengers inside cells, [em1]triggering muscle contractions[em1], nerve signals, and blood clotting, which is why milk, leafy greens, and supplements are part of a healthy diet.[br] [br]Calcium is the fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust. Much of it is calcium carbonate, the stuff of [em3]limestone, marble, chalk, coral reefs, and seashells[em3], built up over millions of years by sea creatures.[br] [br]Heating limestone produces lime, the [em2]key ingredient of cement[em2] and concrete, used in buildings from Roman times to modern skyscrapers. Making cement [em1]releases a significant share[em1] of the world's carbon dioxide emissions. Calcium compounds also make plaster, antacids, baking powder, and toothpaste polish.[br] [br]Very neutron-rich [link]Calcium-48[link] is remarkably stable for its size. Fired as an ion beam at heavy targets, it was used to create every element from [link]Flerovium[link] to [link]Oganesson[link], the [em3]heaviest elements ever made[em3].

name: Scandium
info: [em3]Scandium[em3] has 21 protons and one stable isotope, [link]Scandium-45[link], so all natural scandium is the same nuclide. It was made in [em1]supernova explosions[em1] and by cosmic rays breaking apart heavier nuclei. It's about as common in Earth's crust as [link]Cobalt[link], but it's rarely concentrated and mostly comes as a [em2]byproduct of mining[em2].[br] [br]The world makes only a [em2]few dozen metric tons[em2] of scandium a year, but it's put to good use. Adding just a little to [link]Aluminium[link] makes a [em1]stronger alloy[em1] that has been used in Russian MiG fighter jets, baseball bats, bicycle frames, and lacrosse sticks. Scandium is also used in [em3]metal-halide lamps[em3], which make a white light close enough to sunlight for TV cameras to capture good color.[br] [br]Radioactive [link]Scandium-46[link], with a half-life of about 84 days, is used as a [em1]tracer in oil refineries[em1]. [link]Scandium-45[link] is even being studied for a [em2]nuclear clock[em2] that could, in theory, be far more precise than [link]Caesium[link] clocks.[br] [br]Scandium was found in 1879 by Swedish chemist Lars Fredrik Nilson, and is named after [em3]Scandinavia[em3].

name: Titanium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Titanium[em3] has the [em1]highest strength-to-density ratio[em1] of any metal element. It's [em2]as strong as some steels[em2] but about 45% lighter, and it shrugs off corrosion from seawater and [link]Chlorine[link]. It's the ninth most abundant element in Earth's crust, but separating it from [link]Oxygen[link] is difficult and expensive.[br] [br]About two-thirds of Titanium metal goes into [em3]aircraft frames and jet engines[em3]. The body accepts it so well that [em1]bone grows right onto it[em1], so it's used for hip replacements and dental implants that can last over 30 years, and since it isn't magnetic, patients with them can still get MRI scans. Bicycle frames, watch cases, eyeglasses, and some phones use it too.[br] [br]Far more Titanium, though, about 95% of what's refined, becomes [em2]titanium dioxide (TiO[sub]2[sub])[em2]. It's the [em3]brilliant white pigment[em3] in paint, paper, plastics, and toothpaste, and it blocks ultraviolet light in sunscreen.[br] [br]Titanium is named for the [em1]Titans of Greek mythology[em1]. Powdered Titanium is a fire hazard, and a Titanium fire can't be put out with water or carbon dioxide.

name: Vanadium
info: [em3]Vanadium[em3] has 23 protons, and nearly all natural vanadium (over 99%) is [link]Vanadium-51[link]. The other small percentage is [link]Vanadium-50[link], which is technically radioactive but has a half-life of about 270 quadrillion years, so it's [em1]effectively stable[em1].[br] [br]Vanadium has a moderate neutron-capture cross-section, and the isotopes it forms under neutron exposure have short half-lives, so it's considered a suitable material for the [em2]inner structure of a fusion reactor[em2].[br] [br]About 85% of Vanadium is used as an additive that [em2]significantly increases the strength of steel[em2]. The first large-scale industrial use was in the chassis of the [em1]Ford Model T[em1], and Vanadium steel is also used in axles, bicycle frames, crankshafts, and gears. It strengthens [link]Titanium[link] alloys for jet engines too, and [em3]Vanadium redox batteries[em3] are used for grid energy storage.[br] [br]It was named for Vanadís, another name for the [em3]Norse goddess Freyja[em3], because of its colorful compounds. Sea squirts are known to concentrate Vanadium in their blood cells.

name: Chromium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Chromium[em3] is what [em2]makes stainless steel stainless[em2]. Steel with more than about 11% Chromium forms an invisible oxide layer that [em1]stops rust before it starts[em1], and stainless steel and chrome plating together account for about 85% of Chromium use. South Africa mines nearly half of the world's Chromium ore.[br] [br]Its name comes from [em3]the Greek for 'color'[em3], because its compounds are so vivid. Traces of Chromium make [em2]rubies red and emeralds green[em2], and the very first laser, built in 1960, used a synthetic ruby crystal in which Chromium gave off the light.[br] [br]Polished chrome plating reflects about 70% of visible light, giving [em1]a mirror finish to car parts[em1], faucets, and furniture. Chromium is the [em3]third-hardest element known[em3] after [link]Carbon[link] (as diamond) and [link]Boron[link], and Chromium salts are used to tan leather.[br] [br]Its form matters for health. Chromium(III) occurs naturally in food and is sold as a supplement, while [em2]hexavalent chromium is highly toxic[em2] and causes cancer, as in the contaminated groundwater of Hinkley, California, a case [em1]made famous by a Hollywood film[em1].

name: Manganese
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Manganese[em3] is essential to the air we breathe: a cluster of Manganese atoms in plants is what [em2]splits water to release[em2] [link]Oxygen[link] during photosynthesis. In your body, about 12 milligrams of it [em1]help dozens of enzymes work[em1], and nuts, grains, and tea supply plenty.[br] [br]Steel is where [em3]85 to 90% of Manganese[em3] ends up. It removes [link]Sulfur[link] and Oxygen that would make steel brittle and makes it tougher, and steel with over 12% Manganese [em2]takes a beating in rail crossings[em2] and rock crushers. Manganese also stiffens the [link]Aluminium[link] in drink cans and goes into alkaline batteries. South Africa holds about 80% of known land reserves.[br] [br]Parts of the ocean floor are scattered with [em1]potato-sized Manganese nodules[em1], about 29% Manganese and also rich in [link]Nickel[link] and [link]Cobalt[link]. One estimate put them at 500 billion metric tons, but mining them is still being researched and debated.[br] [br]Too much inhaled Manganese, as in some miners and welders, causes manganism, [em3]a nerve disorder resembling Parkinson's disease[em3]. Potassium permanganate, [em2]a deep purple salt[em2], is a common disinfectant.

name: Iron
info: [em3]Iron[em3] is a widely used metal that's the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust. Extracting usable metal from ores containing Iron requires kilns or furnaces capable of reaching 1,500°C (2,730°F), about 500°C (900°F) higher than that required to smelt [link]Copper[link]. Humans first developed this technology around 4,000 years ago, leading to the [em2]Iron Age[em2].[br] [br]Iron is the [em1]heaviest element created by stellar fusion[em1]. Inside the core of stars fusing lighter elements to make heavier ones releases net energy, but Iron is the first element that when fused consumes energy. All elements heavier than Iron are either produced in [em3]supernova explosions[em3] or by means other than stellar fusion.[br] [br]Iron regularly forms various compounds with [link]Oxygen[link]. When metals [em1]rust[em1] it is the Iron combining with Oxygen to form [em3]Iron(III) Oxide (Fe[sub]2[sub]O[sub]3[sub])[em3]. The same affinity for Oxygen is why human blood is red; Iron in [em2]Hemoglobin[em2] is how red blood cells hold Oxygen for delivery to cells all around the body.

name: Cobalt
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Cobalt[em3] has been used for thousands of years to make [em2]deep blue glass and glazes[em2], including the blue of Ming dynasty porcelain. Its name comes from [em1]kobold, German for goblin[em1], because miners blamed its toxic ores for 'stealing' the [link]Copper[link] and [link]Silver[link] they expected.[br] [br]Today Cobalt is a key metal for lithium-ion batteries. Lithium cobalt oxide, first sold in 1991, [em3]powers most phones and laptops[em3], and many electric vehicle batteries use Cobalt too, though manufacturers are cutting back. Over 300,000 metric tons are produced a year, more than 80% in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where mining has been [em2]linked to child labor[em2] and dangerous conditions. Cobalt superalloys also [em1]withstand the heat inside jet engines[em1].[br] [br]Cobalt sits at the [em3]center of vitamin B12[em3], which only microbes can make. Cattle and sheep grazing on Cobalt-poor soils fall sick, while [em2]too much Cobalt can damage the heart[em2].[br] [br]Radioactive [link]Cobalt-60[link] gives off strong gamma rays that [em1]treat cancer and sterilize[em1] medical supplies and food.

name: Nickel
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Nickel[em3] is one of only four elements that are [em2]magnetic at room temperature[em2], along with [link]Iron[link], [link]Cobalt[link], and [link]Gadolinium[link]. Earth's core is thought to be [em1]mostly Iron and Nickel[em1], and so are many metal meteorites.[br] [br][link]Nickel-62[link] has the [em3]most tightly bound nucleus[em3] of any nuclide, even more than [link]Iron-56[link]. Yet Iron is far more common in the universe, because the Nickel made inside massive stars is mostly [link]Nickel-56[link], which decays into Iron. That decay is what [em2]keeps supernovae glowing for months[em2] after they explode.[br] [br]About 3.9 million metric tons are mined each year, two-thirds in Indonesia, and [em1]about 68% goes into stainless steel[em1]. Nickel batteries powered early hybrid cars, and Nickel-rich cathodes are in many electric vehicle batteries today. Nickel also plates faucets, wraps electric guitar strings, and makes up [em3]25% of the US five-cent coin[em3] that bears its name.[br] [br]Nickel is the [em2]most common contact allergen[em2] in the world, often causing rashes from jewelry and belt buckles. Nickel-[link]Titanium[link] alloys [em1]'remember' their shape[em1] and spring back after bending, useful in eyeglass frames and medical stents.

name: Copper
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Copper[em3] was one of the first metals people ever used, and alloyed with [link]Tin[link] it made bronze, [em1]giving the Bronze Age its name[em1] around 3500 BC. It's one of only a few metals with a natural color other than gray or silver, and it weathers to [em2]the green patina of the Statue of Liberty[em2].[br] [br]Copper conducts electricity better than any metal except [link]Silver[link], at a fraction of the cost, so [em3]about 60% becomes electrical wire[em3]. The world mines about 23 million metric tons a year, led by Chile. A battery electric car holds [em1]about 91 kg of Copper[em1], nearly four times as much as a gasoline car, and [em2]about 80% of all Copper ever mined[em2] is still in use.[br] [br]Your body needs Copper for enzymes that use [link]Oxygen[link], and some animals use it the way we use [link]Iron[link]: horseshoe crabs, octopuses, and many snails carry Oxygen with a Copper protein, [em3]giving them blue blood[em3]. Copper surfaces also [em1]kill many germs[em1].[br] [br]Brass is Copper alloyed with [link]Zinc[link], and radioactive [link]Copper-62[link] is used as a [em2]tracer in PET scans[em2].

name: Zinc
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Zinc[em3] is the [em2]fourth most used metal[em2] in the world, after [link]Iron[link], [link]Aluminium[link], and [link]Copper[link], at about 13 million metric tons a year. More than half of it is used for galvanizing, [em1]coating steel so the Zinc corrodes first[em1] and the steel underneath doesn't rust. Fences, bridges, car bodies, and roofs are protected this way.[br] [br]Zinc is the second most abundant trace metal in your body after Iron, about 2 to 4 grams. Over 300 enzymes need it, and it's important for the immune system, growth, and the senses of taste and smell. [em3]Zinc deficiency affects about two billion people[em3] in the developing world. Zinc lozenges may [em2]shorten a cold[em2], but they don't prevent one.[br] [br]Zinc oxide is a white pigment, a [em1]sunscreen that blocks UV light[em1], and a diaper rash cream. Zinc pyrithione fights dandruff in shampoos. Zinc is the [em3]negative electrode in alkaline batteries[em3], and alloyed with Copper it makes brass.[br] [br]From 1982 until production ended in 2025, the US penny was [em2]about 97.5% Zinc[em2] with a thin coat of Copper. Zinc [em1]burns with a bluish-green flame[em1].

name: Gallium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Gallium[em3] is a soft silvery metal that [em1]melts in your hand[em1], at just 29.8°C (85.6°F). Unlike [link]Mercury[link] it isn't very toxic, and Gallium alloys like Galinstan replace Mercury in some thermometers. It stays liquid up to about 2,400°C, one of the widest liquid ranges of any element, and like water it [em2]expands when it freezes[em2].[br] [br]Gallium is never found pure and comes mainly as a byproduct of processing [link]Aluminium[link] ore. Only about 450 metric tons are made a year, and [em3]China produced 98% of it[em3] in 2024, making it a strategic material.[br] [br]That's because nearly all of it goes into semiconductors. Gallium nitride made the first [em1]bright blue LEDs[em1], an invention that won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics and made white LED lighting possible, and it's now in compact phone chargers. Gallium arsenide, made with [link]Arsenic[link], runs radio chips in phones and [em2]solar cells on satellites[em2].[br] [br]In the body Gallium ions behave somewhat like [link]Iron[link], and radioactive [link]Gallium-68[link] is used in [em3]PET scans that locate tumors[em3].

name: Germanium
info: [em3]Germanium[em3] is one of the [em2]purest materials ever made[em2]: zone refining leaves about one impurity atom in 10 billion. Like water, Germanium [em1]expands when it freezes[em1]. Pure crystals can even grow metal 'whiskers' that shorted out early transistors.[br] [br]The first [em2]transistors[em2], built in 1947, were made of Germanium, which was the [em3]basis of all semiconductor electronics[em3] until the early 1970s when [link]Silicon[link] took over. Germanium transistors powered early [em1]guitar fuzz pedals[em1], and some audio circuits still prefer Germanium diodes for their smoother clipping.[br] [br]Today most Germanium goes into [em1]fiber optic cables[em1], infrared lenses for thermal cameras, and a catalyst for making PET plastic. Germanium also underlies Mars rover solar cells, and ultra-pure crystals detect gamma rays in [em2]searches for dark matter[em2].[br] [br]Germanium supplements were once sold as cancer treatments, but there is no evidence they work, and long-term users of one injectable form developed [em1]kidney damage[em1].

name: Arsenic
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Arsenic[em3] has been called the [em1]'king of poisons'[em1]. Its oxide is nearly tasteless, and before reliable tests were developed in the 1830s it was a favorite of murderers. Today the larger threat is natural Arsenic in groundwater: an estimated [em2]57 million people in the Bengal basin[em2] of Bangladesh and India drink water above the World Health Organization's limit, raising their risk of cancer.[br] [br]Arsenic is a metalloid, sitting below [link]Phosphorus[link] and above [link]Antimony[link] in the periodic table, and in the body it can stand in for Phosphorus, which is part of why it's toxic. At normal pressure it [em3]turns straight from solid to gas[em3] without melting, giving off a garlic-like smell.[br] [br]Its biggest uses are [em1]in car batteries and ammunition[em1], where it strengthens [link]Lead[link], and in [link]Gallium[link] arsenide semiconductors for [em2]LEDs and phone chips[em2]. It was once widely used to preserve wood, until a 2004 ban on consumer uses. Arsenic trioxide is an approved [em3]treatment for a form of leukemia[em3].

name: Selenium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Selenium[em3] is a nutrient with a [em2]narrow safe range[em2]. Your body holds about 13 to 20 milligrams, built into enzymes that protect cells from damage and that activate thyroid hormone. But [em1]more than about 400 micrograms a day[em1] can cause selenosis, with garlic breath and hair loss. Just [em3]a few Brazil nuts[em3] can provide a full day's supply.[br] [br]Grey Selenium [em2]conducts electricity better in light[em2] than in the dark, so it was used in early light meters and photocopiers, and the [em1]first solid-state solar cell[em1], in 1876, was made with Selenium. Amorphous Selenium still detects X-rays in flat-panel medical imagers.[br] [br]Selenium usually replaces [link]Sulfur[link] in metal sulfide ores and is mostly recovered as a byproduct of [link]Copper[link] refining. About half goes into glass, where it [em3]cancels the green tint[em3] from [link]Iron[link] or turns the glass red. Selenium sulfide [em2]fights dandruff in some shampoos[em2].[br] [br]Selenium is [em1]named for the Moon[em1], from the Greek selene, as a partner to [link]Tellurium[link], [em3]named for the Earth[em3], which sits just below it on the periodic table.

name: Bromine
info: [em3]Bromine[em3] is one of only two elements that are [em1]liquid at room temperature[em1], along with [link]Mercury[link]. This reddish-brown liquid boils at just 59°C and gives off a [em3]harsh choking vapor[em3]. Frozen at -195°C it's pale yellow, and squeezed to 55 gigapascals it becomes a [em2]metal[em2].[br] [br][em2]Seawater is about 65 parts per million Bromine[em2], and the Dead Sea is rich enough to be a major source. The oceans release an estimated 1 to 2 million tons of bromoform a year, and organic Bromine compounds are [em1]the most common organohalides in nature[em1].[br] [br]Your own immune cells use it: eosinophils [em3]prefer bromide to chloride[em3] when killing parasites. Potassium bromide was the [em1]only effective epilepsy drug[em1] until 1912, but large doses cause 'bromism' sickness.[br] [br]More than half of all Bromine goes into [em2]flame retardants[em2]. It was also added to leaded gasoline, and as brominated vegetable oil to citrus sodas, until the [em3]US banned it in food in 2024[em3]. Bromine atoms high in the atmosphere [em1]destroy ozone[em1], which has led to restrictions on methyl bromide.

name: Krypton
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Krypton[em3] is a noble gas that makes up [em2]about 1 part per million of the air[em2], and its name is [em1]Greek for 'the hidden one'[em1]. It's extracted from liquid air along with [link]Neon[link] and [link]Xenon[link], and despite its reputation as inert it can be forced into compounds like krypton difluoride.[br] [br]From 1960 to 1983 [em3]the official length of the meter[em3] was defined as 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of the orange-red light given off by [link]Krypton-86[link] atoms, until a definition based on the speed of light replaced it.[br] [br]Krypton fills some energy-efficient lamps, photographic flashes, and the gaps in insulated windows. Since it's cheaper than Xenon, SpaceX uses it as [em2]propellant for the ion thrusters[em2] of its Starlink satellites. Krypton fluoride lasers are used in [em1]fusion energy research[em1].[br] [br]Radioactive [link]Krypton-85[link] is released when used nuclear fuel is reprocessed, so detecting it in the air has helped reveal [em3]secret nuclear programs[em3]. [link]Krypton-81[link], made by cosmic rays, dates very old groundwater. Comic book hero Superman's home planet, Krypton, [em2]borrowed the element's name[em2].

name: Rubidium
info: [em3]Rubidium[em3] is a very soft silvery metal that melts at just 39°C. It's the first alkali metal [em1]denser than water[em1], and it [em2]reacts explosively[em2] with it. Its flame is nearly the same purple as [link]Potassium[link]'s, so telling them apart takes a spectroscope. Rubidium silver iodide has the [em1]highest room-temperature conductivity of any ionic crystal[em1].[br] [br]In 1995, cooling [link]Rubidium-87[link] atoms close to absolute zero created a [em2]Bose-Einstein condensate[em2], a Nobel Prize-winning state of matter. Rubidium is also used in [em1]atomic clocks[em1] for telecom equipment and satellite navigation. Rubidium-87 is radioactive and decays into [link]Strontium-87[link], so geologists use the ratio to [em3]date rocks[em3].[br] [br]The synthetic [link]Rubidium-82[link] lasts only about 76 seconds, yet it's used in [em3]PET scans[em3] of the heart and of brain tumors, since Rubidium builds up in tumor tissue.[br] [br]Rubidium behaves like [link]Potassium[link] in the body, and a 70 kg person holds about 0.36 grams of it. Only 2 to 4 tons of Rubidium compounds are produced each year, mostly from the mineral [em2]lepidolite[em2].

name: Strontium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Strontium[em3] gives fireworks and road flares their [em1]brilliant red color[em1]. It's a soft, reactive metal, the 15th most abundant element on Earth, and chemically so similar to [link]Calcium[link] that the body treats them alike, [em2]storing Strontium in bones[em2].[br] [br]That similarity is behind its most famous danger. [link]Strontium-90[link] is a product of nuclear fission and one of the [em3]most worrying parts of nuclear fallout[em3], because once absorbed it lodges in bone for years. Fallout from 1950s bomb tests [em1]could be measured in children's baby teeth[em1]. The same bone-seeking habit lets [link]Strontium-89[link] [em2]ease pain from cancers[em2] that have spread to bone.[br] [br]Glass for color TV picture tubes, which blocked X-rays, once took about 75% of US Strontium. Today Strontium aluminate makes [em3]glow-in-the-dark toys[em3] and signs shine for hours, and Strontium chloride is in some toothpastes for sensitive teeth.[br] [br]Atomic clocks built on [link]Strontium-87[link] are so precise that Strontium is a leading candidate for a [em1]new definition of the second[em1]. [link]Rubidium-87[link] decays into Strontium-87, which geologists use to date rocks.

name: Yttrium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Yttrium[em3] is one of [em2]four elements named after the same small Swedish village[em2], Ytterby, whose quarry yielded a mineral full of new elements, along with [link]Ytterbium[link], [link]Terbium[link], and [link]Erbium[link]. It's so chemically close to the lanthanides that it's counted among the [em1]rare earth elements[em1].[br] [br]Yttrium oxide was the [em3]red phosphor in color TV tubes[em3], and Yttrium aluminium garnet (YAG) is everywhere today: in white LEDs, and, doped with [link]Neodymium[link], in the [em2]Nd:YAG lasers used in surgery[em2], manufacturing, and tattoo removal.[br] [br]In 1987 Yttrium barium copper oxide (YBCO) became the first material to [em1]superconduct above liquid nitrogen's boiling point[em1], so it could be cooled cheaply rather than with liquid [link]Helium[link]. It's now used in superconducting cables and magnets.[br] [br]Radioactive [link]Yttrium-90[link] is injected as tiny beads into the blood vessels feeding liver tumors to [em3]irradiate them from inside[em3]. Yttrium also strengthens zirconia for ceramic dental crowns and is part of the YInMn Blue pigment.

name: Zirconium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Zirconium[em3] is nearly [em2]transparent to neutrons[em2], so Zirconium alloys form [em1]the tubes that hold nuclear fuel[em1] in reactors. That requires removing its near-twin [link]Hafnium[link], which absorbs neutrons hundreds of times better and is always mixed in with Zirconium in nature.[br] [br]Most Zirconium is never turned into metal. About 900,000 metric tons of [em3]the mineral zircon[em3] are mined a year, mostly in Australia and South Africa, and much of it makes ceramics and tiles white and opaque. Cubic zirconia, crystallized Zirconium dioxide, is the [em2]most popular imitation diamond[em2], and the same material makes tough white dental crowns and ceramic knives.[br] [br]Zircon crystals take in [link]Uranium[link] when they form but reject [link]Lead[link], so any Lead inside one came from Uranium decay. That makes zircon a [em1]superb geologic clock[em1]: zircons from Western Australia about 4.4 billion years old are the [em3]oldest pieces of Earth[em3] ever found.[br] [br]Zirconium powder is highly flammable and was once used in [em2]old photographic flashbulbs[em2]. It has no known role in the body, which holds about 250 mg.

name: Niobium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Niobium[em3] is the [em2]best elemental superconductor[em2], losing all electrical resistance below 9.2 K, a higher temperature than any other element at normal pressure. Wire made of Niobium and [link]Titanium[link] is wound into the magnets of [em1]most MRI scanners[em1] and of the Large Hadron Collider.[br] [br]About 90% of Niobium goes into steel. Less than 0.1% makes high-strength steel for [em3]gas pipelines, cars, and bridges[em3] noticeably stronger and lighter. Brazil supplies [em2]about 90% of the world's Niobium[em2], mostly from two mines. Niobium superalloys also stand up to the heat in jet and rocket engines.[br] [br]Niobium is hypoallergenic, and anodizing it creates a thin oxide film that [em1]shimmers in iridescent colors[em1], making it popular for jewelry, piercings, and commemorative coins.[br] [br]Niobium is so chemically similar to [link]Tantalum[link] that [em3]the two were long confused[em3], and for over a century it was also called columbium. It's named after Niobe, [em2]daughter of Tantalus in Greek myth[em2].

name: Molybdenum
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Molybdenum[em3] is [em1]essential to nearly all life[em1]. Bacteria use it in the enzyme nitrogenase to [em2]pull nitrogen from the air[em2] and turn it into ammonia, the starting point for the [link]Nitrogen[link] in every protein. Your body uses it in a handful of enzymes, and legumes, grains, and nuts supply plenty.[br] [br]It melts at 2,623°C, the sixth-highest of any natural element, and barely expands when heated, so [em3]about 80% goes into steel alloys[em3] for strong, heat-resistant parts like engine components, pipelines, and tools. About 250,000 metric tons are mined a year, led by China, the US, and Chile.[br] [br]Molybdenum disulfide is a [em1]slippery solid lubricant[em1] in greases and engines, and Molybdenum X-ray targets are used for [em2]mammogram breast imaging[em2].[br] [br]Its name comes from [em3]the Greek for 'lead'[em3], because its ore was confused with [link]Lead[link] ore. Radioactive [link]Molybdenum-99[link] decays into [link]Technetium[link], the [em1]most widely used medical imaging isotope[em1], so hospitals receive 'technetium generators' that let them draw it off fresh as needed.

name: Technetium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Technetium[em3] is the [em2]lightest element with no stable isotopes[em2], and the [em1]first element made artificially[em1], in 1937 by Italian scientists. Its name comes from the Greek for 'artificial'. Only traces exist naturally on Earth, from the spontaneous fission of [link]Uranium[link], but in 1952 it was spotted in the light of red giant stars. It couldn't have survived there since the stars formed, so it was proof that [em3]stars forge heavy elements[em3].[br] [br]Technetium is a [em2]workhorse of medical imaging[em2]. Its short-lived excited form, Technetium-99m, gives off gamma rays that cameras can see, and it's used in [em1]about ten million diagnostic procedures a year[em1] to image the heart, bones, brain, and other organs. Hospitals make it on site from [link]Molybdenum-99[link], so the world depends on a handful of reactors to make the Molybdenum.[br] [br][link]Technetium-99[link] is a long-lived product of nuclear fission, about 6% of the fission of [link]Uranium-235[link], making it a [em3]significant part of nuclear waste[em3]. Researchers have turned it into stable [link]Ruthenium-100[link] by bombarding it with neutrons, [em2]a possible way to clean up[em2] that waste.

name: Ruthenium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Ruthenium[em3] is a rare, hard, white member of the [em2]platinum group of metals[em2], with [link]Platinum[link], [link]Osmium[link], and others. It makes up only about 100 parts per trillion of Earth's crust, and [em1]only about 30 metric tons are mined a year[em1], mostly in South Africa. It doesn't tarnish, and even aqua regia can't dissolve it.[br] [br]The biggest use of Ruthenium is in electronics: electrical contacts, chip resistors, and [em3]ultra-thin layers in hard drives[em3] that help pack data more densely. A little added to [link]Titanium[link] [em2]greatly improves its corrosion resistance[em2].[br] [br]Ruthenium is also a powerful catalyst. Ruthenium catalysts developed by American chemist Robert Grubbs made a reaction called olefin metathesis practical for making drugs and plastics, and earned a share of the [em1]2005 Nobel Prize in Chemistry[em1]. Ruthenium dyes have been used in [em3]experimental solar cells[em3].[br] [br]It was discovered in 1844 at Kazan, Russia, and named after Ruthenia, [em2]the Latin name for Russia[em2]. Ruthenium metal is inert, but its tetroxide is highly toxic and volatile, much like Osmium's.

name: Rhodium
info: [em3]Rhodium[em3] has 45 protons and only one stable isotope, [link]Rhodium-103[link], which makes up 100% of natural Rhodium. It's one of the [em1]rarest elements in Earth's crust[em1] with less than one part per billion. The world produces only about 30 metric tons a year, mostly in South Africa.[br] [br]About 80% of it goes into [em1]catalytic converters[em1], where Rhodium helps [em2]reduce nitrogen oxide emissions[em2]. Its price has swung from under $700 per troy ounce in 2016 to nearly $30,000 in 2021.[br] [br]Rhodium also has a job in nuclear power. [em2]Rhodium neutron detectors[em2] measure neutron flux levels in reactors, and each of the three reactors at Palo Verde has over 300 of them to give a [em2]3D picture of reactivity[em2]. Rhodium is also a [em1]fission product[em1] of [link]Uranium-235[link], but recovering it from used fuel is complex and expensive.[br] [br]Rhodium is [em3]electroplated[em3] onto white [link]Gold[link] and [link]Platinum[link] jewelry for a reflective finish. It was discovered in 1803 by English chemist William Hyde Wollaston and named from the Greek [em3]rhodon[em3], 'rose', for the color of one of its compounds.

name: Palladium
info: [em3]Palladium[em3] absorbs [link]Hydrogen[link] at room temperature, so membranes of it make high-purity hydrogen, and it was a key part of the controversial late-1980s [em2]cold fusion[em2] experiments.[br] [br]The biggest use of Palladium by far is [em1]catalytic converters[em1]. It's also used for [em3]electrodes in ceramic capacitors[em3], in pacemakers, spark plugs, and blood sugar test strips, and, since 1939, in white gold jewelry as an alternative to [link]Platinum[link]. Palladium chloride turns carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide, which makes it useful in CO detectors.[br] [br]Palladium chloride was once prescribed for [em2]tuberculosis[em2]. During World War II, when Platinum was a strategic resource, many jewelry bands were made of Palladium, and the Soviet Union minted a [em1]25-ruble Palladium coin[em1]. In 2001 Ford stockpiled Palladium and [em2]lost nearly a billion dollars[em2] when prices fell.[br] [br]People allergic to Palladium often react to [link]Nickel[link] too. English chemist William Hyde Wollaston identified it in 1802 and [em1]named it after the asteroid Pallas[em1].

name: Silver
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Silver[em3] has the [em1]highest electrical conductivity[em1] of any element and the highest thermal conductivity of any metal, and it's the most reflective metal for visible light. It tarnishes black only when it meets [link]Sulfur[link] in the air. Its symbol Ag comes from the Latin argentum, [em2]which also named Argentina[em2].[br] [br]For thousands of years [em3]Silver was money[em3]. Coins, tableware, and jewelry spread it across the world, and from the 1500s Silver from mines in Spanish America [em1]flowed into global trade[em1] as far as China.[br] [br]Today about 26,000 metric tons are mined a year, led by Mexico, Peru, and China. Silver once went largely into photographic film, but [em2]solar panels are now one of its biggest uses[em2], along with electronics, brazing, and mirrors.[br] [br]Silver ions kill bacteria, so Silver coats [em3]wound dressings and catheters[em3] and odor-resistant clothing, and it was used to keep water fresh long before germs were understood. Swallowing too much Silver over time can cause argyria, which [em1]turns the skin permanently blue-gray[em1].

name: Cadmium
info: [em3]Cadmium[em3] is unusually resistant to corrosion, so some of it goes into [em2]plating aircraft steel[em2]. In 2009, 86% went into [em3]batteries[em3], mostly rechargeable nickel-cadmium cells. Cadmium compounds make [em1]red, orange, and yellow pigments[em1], Cadmium telluride makes solar cells, and Cadmium in reactor control rods [em2]absorbs neutrons[em2].[br] [br][em1]Cadmium is toxic.[em1] Japan's itai-itai disease was linked to Cadmium-contaminated rice. Its biological half-life in humans is 20 to 40 years, and smokers have 4 to 5 times the blood Cadmium of non-smokers. In 2022 Consumer Reports found it in [em3]all 28 dark chocolates[em3] it tested.[br] [br]It's about 650 times scarcer than [link]Zinc[link] in Earth's crust and mostly a by-product of Zinc production. Phosphate fertilizers carry it into crops, while willow and poplar trees can pull it from soil. Cadmium-plated tools were [em2]banned from the U-2 and SR-71 programs[em2] for contaminating [link]Titanium[link], and the EU's RoHS directive now bans it in electronics.

name: Indium
info: [em3]Indium[em3] is so soft that it can be cut with a knife, and bending it makes a [em1]high-pitched cry[em1]. It melts at just 157°C, and it dissolves in liquid [link]Mercury[link] at over 50% by mass, more than any other metal.[br] [br]Indium's biggest use is Indium tin oxide, a transparent [em3]conductive coating on glass for flat-panel displays[em3]. LCD monitors and TVs account for about half of Indium use. Indium compounds also make [em1]LEDs, laser diodes[em1], and thin-film solar cells. Alloys that melt between 50 and 100°C trigger fire sprinklers, and Galinstan, a [link]Gallium[link]-Indium-[link]Tin[link] alloy, replaces Mercury in some thermometers.[br] [br]In World War II, Indium coated bearings in [em1]high-performance aircraft engines[em1]. It's also in [em2]YInMn Blue[em2], the first new inorganic blue pigment in about 200 years.[br] [br]Indium is about as rare in Earth's crust as [link]Silver[link] and is produced only as a by-product of other metals, mostly [link]Zinc[link]. [em3]Less than 1% is recycled.[em3] It has no known biological role and is toxic when inhaled or injected, but poorly absorbed when swallowed.

name: Tin
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Tin[em3] alloyed with [link]Copper[link] makes bronze, and that combination [em1]gave its name to the Bronze Age[em1]. Tin ores are rare and scattered, so ancient trade networks carried Tin long distances to bronze-making cities, from mines [em2]as far off as Cornwall[em2] in Britain.[br] [br]Today about half of all Tin goes into [em3]solder that holds electronics together[em3]. Tin-plated steel makes the [em1]familiar 'tin can'[em1], window glass is made by floating molten glass on a bath of molten Tin, and pewter is mostly Tin. China, Indonesia, Peru, and Bolivia are leading producers.[br] [br]Bending a bar of Tin makes a [em2]crackling 'tin cry'[em2] as its crystals slip. In the cold, ordinary white Tin can [em3]slowly crumble into gray powder[em3], an effect called tin pest.[br] [br]Tin melts at only 232°C. Tin droplets blasted by lasers produce the [em1]extreme ultraviolet light[em1] used to print the smallest features on today's most advanced computer chips, and [link]Niobium[link]-Tin superconducting wire forms the magnets of the ITER fusion reactor.

name: Antimony
info: [em3]Antimony[em3] is a brittle silvery metalloid. Its pentafluoride is the key ingredient of [em2]fluoroantimonic acid[em2], a superacid, and its hydride, stibine, falls apart at room temperature. Antimony also goes into [link]Indium[link] antimonide infrared detectors and [em1]phase-change memory[em1].[br] [br]About half of the world's Antimony goes into [em2]flame retardants[em2], and a third into [em3]lead-acid batteries[em3]. It also [em1]hardens [link]Lead[link][em1] in sailboat keels, bullets, solder, type metal, and pewter, clears bubbles from glass, and steadies friction in brake pads.[br] [br]Antimony's sulfide mineral, [em3]stibnite[em3], was used as the eye cosmetic 'kohl' in predynastic Egypt as early as about [em1]3100 BCE[em1], and its symbol Sb comes from the Latin [em3]stibium[em3]. Doctors once prescribed an [em2]Antimony pill[em2] that could be swallowed, passed, and used again.[br] [br]Antimony and many of its compounds are toxic, like its [em2]group 15[em2] companion [link]Arsenic[link], but far less so. It can leach from PET plastic bottles into drinks.

name: Tellurium
info: [em3]Tellurium[em3] has 52 protons and eight naturally occurring isotopes. Six are stable, and two, [link]Tellurium-128[link] and [link]Tellurium-130[link], are radioactive with extremely long half-lives. Tellurium-128 has [em1]the longest known half-life of any radionuclide[em1]: trillions of trillions of years.[br] [br]Tellurium is [em2]far more common in the universe than on Earth[em2], where its abundance in the crust (~1 part per billion) is comparable to [link]Platinum[link]. Astronomers have seen Tellurium [em2]produced in neutron star mergers[em2].[br] [br]In 2022 about 40% of Tellurium went into [em1]solar panels[em1] made with [link]Cadmium[link] telluride (CdTe), and about 30% into thermoelectric devices. It's also used in [em3]rewritable optical discs and in phase-change memory chips[em3]. Bombarding it with neutrons is the most common way to make [link]Iodine-131[link], which treats some thyroid conditions.[br] [br]Tellurium is mostly a by-product of [link]Copper[link] refining, where 1000 tons of copper ore yields only about one kilogram. Its name comes from the Latin [em3]tellus[em3], meaning 'earth'.

name: Iodine
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Iodine[em3] is the [em2]heaviest element commonly needed by living things[em2]. Your thyroid gland uses it to make the hormones that control metabolism, growth, and brain development. Iodine deficiency affects about two billion people and is [em1]the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability[em1], which is why [em3]most table salt is iodized[em3]. Seaweed and seafood are rich natural sources.[br] [br]After nuclear accidents, radioactive [link]Iodine-131[link] in fallout [em2]collects in the thyroid[em2]. Taking [em1]potassium iodide pills[em1] floods the thyroid with ordinary Iodine so it can't absorb the radioactive kind. Doctors also use Iodine-131 to treat thyroid cancer and overactive thyroids.[br] [br]Iodine absorbs X-rays strongly, so its top use is in [em3]X-ray and CT contrast agents[em3]. Chile and Japan produce most of the world's Iodine, from mineral deposits and underground brine. Iodine tinctures disinfect wounds, and Iodine turns starch dark blue, a test used to [em2]spot counterfeit banknotes[em2].[br] [br]Solid Iodine is a shiny gray-black, but when warmed it [em1]gives off a violet vapor[em1], which gave Iodine its name from the Greek for 'violet'.

name: Xenon
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Xenon[em3] is a rare noble gas, [em2]less than 0.1 parts per million[em2] of the air, and only tens of metric tons are produced each year, which makes it expensive. In 1962 it became the [em1]first noble gas made into a compound[em1], overturning the belief that these gases couldn't react at all.[br] [br]Xenon glows a bright blue-white in an electric current, so it fills [em3]camera flashes and strobe lights[em3] and some car headlights. It's also the main propellant for [em2]spacecraft ion thrusters[em2], including those of NASA's Dawn probe.[br] [br]Breathed in, Xenon [em1]works as a general anesthetic[em1], more potent than nitrous oxide, and it reaches the brain without being toxic. It also [em3]makes your voice sound deeper[em3], the opposite of [link]Helium[link]. Hyperpolarized [link]Xenon-129[link] is inhaled to make MRI images of the lungs.[br] [br]Huge tanks of liquid Xenon are used to [em2]search for dark matter[em2]. [link]Xenon-135[link], a fission product, is the most significant neutron absorber in nuclear reactors, and its buildup played a role in the [em1]Chernobyl nuclear disaster[em1].

name: Caesium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Caesium[em3] [em2]defines time itself[em2]. Since 1967 the official second has been 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation from a transition in [link]Caesium-133[link] atoms, and [em1]Caesium atomic clocks[em1] keep the time standards that GPS, phone networks, and the internet rely on.[br] [br]Caesium is the most electropositive element and the [em3]least electronegative stable one[em3]: it reacts with water even at -116°C. It's pale gold and melts at just 28.5°C, so it can [em2]turn liquid on a warm day[em2]. Its name comes from the Latin for 'bluish grey', after the blue lines in its spectrum.[br] [br]Only 5 to 10 metric tons are mined a year, mainly from the Tanco mine in Canada. Its largest use is caesium formate, [em1]a dense drilling fluid[em1] for oil and gas wells.[br] [br]Radioactive [link]Caesium-137[link] is one of the [em3]most significant parts of nuclear fallout[em3], released in large amounts at Chernobyl and Fukushima. The body treats Caesium like [link]Potassium[link], spreading it through soft tissue, and it [em2]builds up in mushrooms and wild game[em2]. Prussian blue helps remove it from the body.

name: Barium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Barium[em3] gets its name from [em1]the Greek for 'heavy'[em1], barys, for the density of its minerals. Its most important compound is barium sulfate, or barite, so dense that most of it, millions of metric tons a year, is ground up and [em2]pumped down oil and gas wells[em2] as drilling mud to hold back high-pressure fluids. China produces more than half of it.[br] [br]Barium blocks X-rays, so patients drink a [em3]chalky 'barium meal'[em3] to make the digestive tract show up in X-ray images. That's safe only because barium sulfate doesn't dissolve: [em1]soluble Barium compounds are poisonous[em1], causing convulsions and paralysis.[br] [br]Barium compounds [em2]burn with a bright green flame[em2], giving fireworks their green colors. Barium titanate is used in capacitors, and Barium is part of YBCO, the first superconductor that worked above the temperature of liquid nitrogen.[br] [br]In 1938 German chemists found Barium among the products of bombarding [link]Uranium[link] with neutrons. It was the key clue that the Uranium nucleus had split in two, [em3]the discovery of nuclear fission[em3].

name: Lanthanum
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Lanthanum[em3] is the first of the lanthanides, [em2]the series of 15 metals named after it[em2], and its name comes from [em1]the Greek for 'to lie hidden'[em1], because it was hidden in another mineral. Despite being called a rare earth, it's [em3]about three times as common as[em3] [link]Lead[link] in Earth's crust.[br] [br]The batteries in many hybrid cars use a Lanthanum-[link]Nickel[link] alloy that soaks up [link]Hydrogen[link], and a single Toyota Prius battery holds [em2]10 to 15 kg of Lanthanum[em2]. Lanthanum oxide makes high-quality glass for [em1]camera and telescope lenses[em1], and Lanthanum catalysts help refine crude oil into gasoline.[br] [br]Lanthanum [em3]binds tightly to phosphate[em3]. As a medicine, Lanthanum carbonate lowers phosphate in the blood of people with kidney failure, and Lanthanum-treated clay strips phosphate from lakes and pools to [em2]starve the algae that feed on it[em2].[br] [br]Mixed with [link]Cerium[link] in 'mischmetal', it makes [em1]the flints in lighters[em1] spark. Some methane-eating bacteria [em3]need Lanthanum to live[em3], though it has no role in the human body.

name: Cerium
info: (DRAFT) [em3]Cerium[em3] is the [em2]most common rare earth[em2], about as abundant in Earth's crust as [link]Copper[link], and it's [em1]named after the dwarf planet Ceres[em1]. It's the only lanthanide that easily forms a +4 ion in water, which makes it easy to separate from the others.[br] [br]Cerium metal [em3]ignites in air at just 65 to 80°C[em3] and sparks when scraped, which is why it's the key ingredient of the mischmetal 'flints' in lighters, along with [link]Lanthanum[link]. Cerium oxide [em2]in catalytic converters[em2] stores and releases [link]Oxygen[link] to burn off carbon monoxide and other pollutants in car exhaust.[br] [br]Cerium oxide is also [em1]the standard polish for glass[em1], from eyeglasses to precision optics. Cerium-doped [link]Yttrium[link] aluminium garnet is the yellow phosphor that turns blue light into [em3]white light in most LED bulbs[em3].[br] [br]Cerium nitrate creams [em2]fight infection in severe burns[em2]. In one famous oscillating reaction, Cerium flips back and forth between two states, making a solution [em1]pulse with color[em1] like a chemical clock.

name: Praseodymium
info: [em3]Praseodymium[em3] is a soft silvery rare earth that [em2]tarnishes fast[em2]: a centimeter-sized sample corrodes away completely in about a year. It's mixed in with other rare earths in ores like bastnäsite and monazite, and China produces over 80% of the world's supply.[br] [br]Together with [link]Neodymium[link], Praseodymium makes [em1]powerful permanent magnets[em1] for electric vehicles and wind turbines. Added to [link]Magnesium[link] it strengthens metal for aircraft engines, and a Praseodymium-[link]Nickel[link] compound has a magnetocaloric effect strong enough to [em2]cool to within a thousandth of a degree of absolute zero[em2].[br] [br]Praseodymium tints glass, enamels, and ceramics yellow, and [em1]didymium glass[em1] goggles protect welders and glassblowers. In some crystals it has [em2]slowed a pulse of light to a few hundred meters per second[em2].[br] [br]Some methane-eating bacteria in volcanic mudpots [em3]need rare earths[em3] to live, and Praseodymium works for them about as well as [link]Lanthanum[link] or [link]Cerium[link].

name: Neodymium
info: [em3]Neodymium[em3] makes the [em1]strongest widely available permanent magnets[em1], Nd[sub]2[sub]Fe[sub]14[sub]B, sold since 1984. They spin electric vehicle motors and wind turbine generators, steer hard drive heads, and drive headphones. A portable brain scanner prototype used them to make a [em2]strong magnetic field without cryogenic cooling[em2].[br] [br]Neodymium salts and glass [em3]change color with the light[em3], so Neodymium glass looks different in daylight than under incandescent bulbs. Mixed with [link]Praseodymium[link] as didymium it makes glasses that protect glassworkers by [em1]blocking the intense yellow sodium glow[em1]. Nd:YAG crystals produce lasers for manufacturing, medicine, and [em2]fusion research[em2].[br] [br][link]Samarium-147[link] decays into [link]Neodymium-143[link] over about 107 billion years, so the ratio between them dates rocks. Neodymium-150 is a candidate for searches for [em1]neutrinoless double beta decay[em1].[br] [br]Neodymium is about as common in Earth's crust as [link]Lanthanum[link], mostly in bastnäsite and monazite, and China refines most of it.

name: Promethium
info: [em3]Promethium[em3] is the only lanthanide with [em2]no stable isotopes[em2]. Only about 500 to 600 grams exist in Earth's crust at any moment, about 560 of them from the fission of [link]Uranium[link] and about 12 from the decay of [link]Europium-151[link], and a pitchblende sample held just [em1]4 parts per quintillion[em1].[br] [br][link]Promethium-147[link] is made in nuclear reactors and its beta rays make phosphors glow. It replaced [link]Radium[link] in [em1]luminous paint[em1] for signal lights, since unlike alpha emitters it doesn't degrade the phosphor, and it was favored over tritium partly for safety. A 1964 atomic battery of about 2 cubic inches used Promethuem's steady beta radiation to produce [em2]few milliwatts of power for roughly five years[em2], and Promethium also gauges thickness by how much radiation passes through a sheet.[br] [br]Its ion is [em3]pink[em3], as are most of its compounds. Output has fallen from about 650 grams a year at Oak Ridge in the 1960s to an estimated 20 to 30 milligrams a year today.[br] [br]Promethium lines have been [em2]reported in the spectra of a few stars[em2]. It has been proposed for portable X-ray sources and space probe power, but [link]Plutonium-238[link] is now the standard.

name: Samarium
info: [em3]Samarium[em3]-[link]Cobalt[link] magnets stay stable above 700°C, while Neodymium magnets give out at 300 to 400°C, so a single F-35 fighter jet carries about [em1]23 kg of them[em1]. Samarium-149 absorbs neutrons with a cross section of [em2]41,000 barns[em2], which helps control nuclear reactors.[br] [br]Samarium(II) ions are [em1]blood-red[em1] in water, and Samarium(II) iodide is a common reducing agent in organic chemistry. Samarium sulfide turns from black to [em3]golden yellow when scratched[em3], and it makes voltage when heated to 150°C, which could suit thermoelectric converters. The silvery metal dulls in air and ignites by itself at 150°C.[br] [br][link]Samarium-153[link], with a half-life of 46 hours, is used in a [em1]drug that targets certain cancers[em1], including osteosarcoma. An adult body holds about 50 micrograms of Samarium, mostly in the liver and kidneys.[br] [br]A Samarium-[link]Gadolinium[link] by-product called [em2]'Lindsay Mix'[em2] served as control rod material in some early reactors. China produces essentially all of the world's usable Samarium, about 700 tons a year.

name: Europium
info: [em3]Europium[em3] is the [em1]most reactive lanthanide metal[em1], reacting even with hot water. It prefers the +2 state more than any other lanthanide, which gives it a larger atomic volume than its neighbors and makes it behave unlike them.[br] [br]Europium makes color. Its [em2]red phosphor[em2] lit color TV tubes from the 1960s, and three-band fluorescent lamps use Europium for both red and blue light. [link]Strontium[link] aluminate doped with [link]Europium[link] and [link]Dysprosium[link] [em3]glows green for hours[em3], replacing older [link]Zinc[link] sulfide glow-in-the-dark phosphors.[br] [br]Trace Europium causes the [em1]intense blue fluorescence of some natural fluorite[em1]. Europium chelates let labs detect biomarkers by waiting for background glow to fade, and Europium-152 and -154 calibrate [em3]gamma ray spectrometers[em3].[br] [br]Europium enters feldspar preferentially, so 'europium anomalies' in rocks reveal how they crystallized. In old, metal-poor stars its abundance traces the [em2]rapid neutron-capture process[em2] that forges heavy elements.

name: Gadolinium
info: [em3]Gadolinium[em3] is ferromagnetic below 20°C and the [em1]most paramagnetic element[em1] above it, so at body temperature no element responds more strongly to magnetism. That makes it the basis of [em2]MRI contrast agents[em2], injected to make tissue stand out.[br] [br]Free Gadolinium ions are [em3]highly toxic[em3], so those agents lock it inside a chelating molecule. In people with kidney failure, though, Gadolinium can still deposit in the brain, bone, and skin.[br] [br][link]Gadolinium-157[link] captures slow neutrons better than any other stable nuclide, about [em1]259,000 barns[em1]. Gadolinium serves as a burnable poison in naval reactors, as emergency shutdown in some CANDU reactors, and helps Super-Kamiokande [em2]detect antineutrinos from supernovae[em2].[br] [br]A Gadolinium-[link]Silicon[link]-[link]Germanium[link] alloy shows a strong magnetocaloric effect up to 27°C, a route to magnetic refrigeration. Gadolinium gallium garnet once made [em3]imitation diamonds[em3] and computer bubble memory, and neutron capture therapy for tumors is under study.

name: Terbium
info: [em3]Terbium[em3]'s ion glows [em2]bright lemon-yellow[em2] from a strong green emission line. Terbium green phosphors, paired with [link]Europium[link] ones in trichromatic lighting, are its largest use, about 340 tons of demand in 2020.[br] [br]Terfenol-D, a Terbium alloy, has the [em1]highest magnetostriction of any alloy[em1], meaning it changes shape in a magnetic field, and it drives actuators, sensors, and naval sonar. Terbium-doped garnets are used in optical isolators, and Terbium stabilizes zirconia in high-temperature fuel cells.[br] [br]Removing Terbium's fourth electron takes a strong oxidizer, because of a [em2]stable half-filled shell[em2]. Terbium(IV) fluoride is a powerful [link]Fluorine[link] source that releases atomic Fluorine when heated. Terbium has even been [em3]detected in the atmosphere of the exoplanet KELT-9b[em3].[br] [br]Terbium-149 is a candidate for [em1]targeted alpha therapy[em1], and since Terbium behaves somewhat like [link]Calcium[link], its glow could serve as a biochemical probe. A deposit discovered off Japan's Minamitori Island in 2018 was said to be [em2]enough for 420 years[em2] of world demand.

name: Dysprosium
info: [em3]Dysprosium[em3] has 66 protons and [em1]seven stable isotopes[em1], led by [link]Dysprosium-164[link] at about 28% of the natural total. It's also very good at [em2]absorbing neutrons[em2], so mixtures of [em3]Dysprosium Oxide (Dy[sub]2[sub]O[sub]3[sub])[em3] and [link]Nickel[link] are used as control rods in nuclear reactors.[br] [br]But dysprosium is best known for its [em1]magnets[em1]. Replacing a bit of the [link]Neodymium[link] in neodymium magnets with dysprosium (up to 6%) helps them keep their magnetism in demanding uses like [em3]electric vehicle motors[em3] and [em3]wind turbine generators[em3]. An electric car can contain up to 100 grams of it.[br] [br]Dysprosium and [link]Holmium[link] have the highest magnetic strengths of any elements, especially at low temperatures. Dysprosium is also in [em2]Terfenol-D[em2], an alloy that changes shape in a magnetic field more than any other known material at room temperature, and is used in [em1]transducers and fuel injectors[em1].[br] [br]Its name comes from the Greek for [em3]'hard to get'[em3] as its discoverer, French chemist Paul Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, needed more than 30 attempts to separate it.

name: Holmium
info: [em3]Holmium[em3] has the [em1]highest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element[em1]. That makes it useful in the [em2]pole pieces of some of the strongest static magnets[em2] ever built.[br] [br]Holmium oxide [em2]changes color with the light[em2]. It looks yellowish in daylight, orange red under some lamps, and pink under others.
